headline: India Takes Forward Six Urea Plants Under NIPU-2026 in Push for Self-Reliance
subheadline: Six brownfield projects of 12.7 lakh tonnes each — replacing units up to 60 years old — aim to narrow the gap between India's ~400 LMT urea demand and domestic output.
body:
• India has taken forward six brownfield urea plants under the National Investment Policy for Urea (NIPU)-2026, with an investment of approximately ₹54,000 crore, the Press Information Bureau said.
  • Each project — in Chennai, Nangal, Shahjahanpur, Panagarh, Gadepan and Jagdishpur — carries an annual installed capacity of 12.7 lakh metric tonnes.
  • Two of the projects replace ageing units: Madras Fertilizers' plant is over 60 years old, and NFL Nangal's is 50-55 years old with capacity of 4.73 LMT a year.
  • India's annual urea consumption is around 400 LMT against production of 293.30 LMT in 2025-26 — the gap the expansion is meant to narrow. The plants are approved projects, not yet operating capacity.

The Government of India has taken forward six new brownfield urea plants under the National Investment Policy for Urea (NIPU)-2026, with an investment of approximately ₹54,000 crore, the Press Information Bureau announced on November 25. The projects span public-sector, private-sector and cooperative enterprises across five states, and the government said more projects will follow.

The six projects

Each project has an annual installed production capacity of 12.7 lakh metric tonnes (LMT). In Chennai, Tamil Nadu, Madras Fertilizers (MFL) will replace an existing unit that is over 60 years old and incurs higher production costs, high energy consumption and safety hazards. In Nangal, Punjab, National Fertilizers (NFL) will replace a plant around 50-55 years old, with present capacity of 4.73 LMT a year, with a modern 12.7 LMT unit. KRIBHCO's cooperative project at Shahjahanpur, Uttar Pradesh, expands a unit commissioned in 1995. Matix Fertilizers will add capacity at Panagarh, West Bengal — so far the state's only urea plant site — alongside its plant commissioned in 2017. Chambal Fertilisers expands its Gadepan complex in Kota, Rajasthan, operational since 1994, and IIPL adds capacity at Jagdishpur, Uttar Pradesh, at a plant established in 1988.

The Hindu BusinessLine reported that the approvals came from 18 proposals received, under the NIPU-2026 policy the Cabinet approved and which was notified on July 30.

Why brownfield, and why now

Brownfield sites come with existing land, utilities, infrastructure, logistics and technical manpower, which the government said enables faster execution and cost efficiency — an estimated ₹225 crore in annual savings, or roughly ₹1,800 crore over eight years. The legacy units make the case plainly: the PIB release notes Nangal operates at 6.498 Gcal per metric tonne, against a weighted industry average of 5.95 and a new energy norm of 5.

The demand gap is the larger driver. India's annual urea consumption stands at around 400 LMT. Domestic production rose from 225 LMT in 2014-15 to a record 314.07 LMT in 2023-24, and stood at 293.30 LMT in 2025-26, while total indigenous reassessed capacity rose from 207.54 LMT a year in 2014-15 to 269.42 LMT in 2026-27. Reducing reliance on imported urea is meant to save foreign exchange and strengthen availability for farmers.

How the investment is structured

With each project estimated at a capital cost norm of around ₹9,000 crore, the six plants account for the roughly ₹54,000 crore total. To support bankability, the framework sets a return on equity band of 12-16 percent — a 12 percent floor and a 16 percent ceiling — alongside a foreign-exchange mitigation mechanism that normalises exchange rates and converts into rupees after four years.

What is still to come

These are approved projects under a new policy, not new production: no completion dates for the six were given in the announcement. Two earlier 12.7 LMT projects remain under execution — the coal-gasification-based Talcher Fertilizer Project in Odisha, expected to complete by December 2027, and Assam Valley Fertilizers at Namrup, announced on March 19, 2025. The earlier New Investment Policy-2012 had already delivered six units of 12.7 LMT each, adding 76.2 LMT of capacity.
diaspora_angle: Expanded domestic urea capacity targets India's fertiliser security and import bill, a cost line that flows through to food prices.

items.text: Madras Fertilizers' plant in Chennai is over 60 years old and will be replaced.
NFL Nangal's plant is 50-55 years old with a current capacity of 4.73 LMT/year, to be replaced by a 12.7 LMT unit.
Brownfield sites enable faster execution and cost efficiency, saving an estimated ₹225 crore annually.
Domestic urea production rose from 225 LMT in 2014-15 to a record 314.07 LMT in 2023-24.
The investment framework sets a return on equity band of 12-16 percent.

dates.event: IIPL plant at Jagdishpur, Uttar Pradesh, established
Chambal Fertilisers' Gadepan complex in Kota, Rajasthan, operational
KRIBHCO's cooperative project at Shahjahanpur, Uttar Pradesh, commissioned
Matix Fertilizers' plant at Panagarh, West Bengal, commissioned
Press Information Bureau announced six new brownfield urea plants

key_takeaways: India is advancing six brownfield urea plants under NIPU-2026 with a ₹54,000 crore investment to boost domestic production.
Each new plant will add 12.7 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) of annual capacity, replacing older units or expanding existing facilities.
The initiative aims to narrow India's urea demand-supply gap and reduce reliance on imports.
Brownfield sites offer faster execution and cost efficiency due to existing infrastructure.
The policy includes a 12-16% return on equity band and a foreign-exchange mitigation mechanism to support investment.
